item.title: Ty Segall does it again
item.dc:creator: admin
item.content:encoded:
In a musical landscape cluttered with predictable releases, Ty Segall's fifteenth studio album "Three Bells" emerges as a refreshing jolt to the system.

Released in January 2024 on Drag City Records, this sprawling 15-track, 66-minute opus represents Segall at his most ambitious and creatively unrestrained. After years of watching artists play it safe, it's invigorating to encounter work that fearlessly pushes boundaries while maintaining cohesion.

What immediately strikes you about "Three Bells" is its meticulous construction. Unlike the freewheeling momentum that typically characterizes Segall's output, this album showcases a measured quality rarely found in his previous work.

"This is an album that sounds like it's had time spent on it. It's brilliantly recorded, pristine and perfectly imperfect."

Uncut

The production, handled by Segall himself alongside Cooper Crain, achieves that elusive balance between polish and raw energy, allowing each instrument room to breathe without sacrificing the psychedelic fuzz that defines Segall's signature sound.

Songs like "The Bell" and "Void" establish this theme early with their shifting time signatures and evolving structures, while more accessible tracks like "My Room" provide brief respites of catchy garage rock amid the experimental sprawl.

The album benefits significantly from contributions by Segall's wife Denée, who co-wrote five songs and lends vocals to "Move," adding another dimension to this already multifaceted work.

Perhaps most impressive is Segall's instrumental versatility throughout the record. While known primarily for his guitar prowess, he handles drums on nearly every track, creating a distinctive rhythmic foundation that ties together the album's diverse sonic explorations. From the prog-rock acoustic entreaty of "The Bell" to the Beck-like experimentation of "Hi Dee Dee" and the extended math-jazz jam of "Denée," Segall demonstrates a musical vocabulary that has expanded far beyond his garage rock origins.

After years of watching artists recycle formulas and chase trends, "Three Bells" stands as a testament to the enduring value of artistic risk-taking. As Paste Magazine observed, "What 'Three Bells' gives us is more than an hour of his musical stream of consciousness roaming wild and free-the results are unpredictable, imperfect and utterly fascinating."

In an era where algorithm-friendly mediocrity often prevails, Segall has crafted something genuinely surprising – a late-career masterpiece that rewards repeated listens and reminds us why we fell in love with adventurous music in the first place.
